newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end narrowly higher before jobs data.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end narrowly higher before jobs data.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices ended narrowly higher on Thursday as traders adjusted positions before the key March employment report due on Friday morning.
The 6-3/4 percent 30-year bond closed at 94-16/32, up 2/32, its yield at 7.07 percent.

U.S. Treasury prices were narrowly lower for most of the session although bills -- at the short end of the maturity spectrum -- turned positive when the Federal Reserve added permanent reserves to the banking system at mid-morning by purchasing bills.

Activity in the intermediate and long end of the curve was just moderate, governed by minor, last-minute positioning before the closely watched monthly employment report, scheduled for release on Friday. Economists polled by Reuters forecast, on average, that U.S. payrolls grew by 196,000 jobs in March, down from 339,000 new jobs in February.

"There was a little bit of buying ahead of the payroll numbers," said Matthew Alexy, chief markets strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston. "There were a couple of forecasts, including ours, saying the (payroll jobs) number could be a bit low, mostly because of special factors."
Alexy said the pre-payroll report action was the opposite of what took place before the February payroll report.

"Last month people worried about a number that could force the Fed into action and they got short," he said. "This month it's the opposite. They're worried about a weaker than expected number that could prompt a short-covering rally."
Credit Suisse First Boston estimates that U.S. payrolls grew by 133,000 jobs in March, Alexy said.
In addition to the job growth numbers, investors will also look at the average workweek and hourly wage data contained in the March payrolls report, analysts said.

Investors are very interested in the average hourly wage statistic because Federal Reserve officials frequently refer to the possibility that tight labor markets will cause potentially inflationary upward pressure on wages.
Average hourly wages are forecast to have risen 0.4 percent in March after a 0.2 percent February gain.
The average workweek is estimated to have been trimmed to 34.8 hours in March from 35.0 hours in February.
Analysts said unexpected strength in any part of the March jobs report could prompt selling.
On Thursday, the Labor Department reported that new claims for jobless benefits rose to 314,000 in the latest week from a revised 313,000 a week earlier.
The report reflected a few more new jobless claims than had been forecast but the Treasury market, already focused on Friday's employment data, did not react to it, analysts said.

At the short end of the maturity curve, three-month bill rates eased three basis points to finish at 5.12 percent. Six-month rates eased one basis point to 5.29 percent and year bill rates eased two basis points to 5.61 percent.
The Fed bought $4.0 billion in bills.
Two-year note prices rose 1/32 to 99-24/32, yielding 6.39 percent.
The five-year note was unchanged at 99-20/32, yielding 6.71 percent and ten-year notes rose 2/32 to 95-22/32 to yield 6.86 percent.
